newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Germany make slow progress on EU reform.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany make slow progress on EU reform.

text.p: France and Germany inched slowly towards narrowing differences on European Union reform on Wednesday, reporting progress on interior and justice affairs, but wide divergences remained over the European Parliament.

Foreign ministers Herve de Charette and Klaus Kinkel told reporters that Paris and Bonn were determined to speed up a slow-moving Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) to overhaul the Union's institutions without dictating to their EU partners.

After an informal brainstorming summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Saturday, President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl would launch a joint initiative ahead of a formal summit in the Irish capital in December, they said.

De Charette said it was vital to stick to the timetable of concluding the IGC with a new treaty making a common foreign and security policy more effective and improving the functioning of EU decision-making by next June so that negotiations to admit central European and Mediterranean states could begin on time.
"The Franco-German booster will have to accelerate the process," he said.
Both ministers reported progress on introducing majority voting in home and justice affairs, including visa and asylum policy and the fight against drugs and organised crime.

Kinkel said they would be brought fully under European Community law, giving the European Commission and the European Parliament a major say. But French ministers said they sought a new procedure giving national parliaments a voice and allowing the council of EU ministers to initiate action.

There was little apparent movement on the two main issues on which France and Germany disagree: the powers of an EU foreign policy "tsar" and the roles of the European Parliament and of national parliaments in a reformed Union.

Kinkel said the European Parliament was the question on which they were widest apart. Bonn wants to extend its powers of co-decision on EU legislation while Paris opposes giving the Strasbourg-based assembly any increased role.

They agreed on the need to boost the EU's fledgling common foreign and security policy by appointing a senior official to represent the bloc internationally and head a policy unit answerable to the Union's foreign ministers.

But while France wants a "high representative" of the level of former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt or former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez reporting directly to heads of state and government, Germany wants a lower-level "general secretary" reporting to foreign ministers.
Kinkel said he was sure they would manage to harmonise their positions soon.

Both countries agree on the need to change the weighted voting system to give the big member states more clout relative to the smaller ones as a prelude to the enlargement of the EU to take in former communist Central European states.
But a survey this week showed that Germany's government ministries do not yet agree among themselves on which areas qualified majority voting should be extended to.
